The proposed reform of the Medical Device Regulation and its implications for AI-enabled medical devices in the EU
desc: The European Medical Device Regulations have been criticized for imposing disproportionate barriers to innovation due to excessive regulatory requirements. In response, the European Commission proposed amendments to key regulations in December 2025. The reforms aim to eliminate double regulation, reduce documentation requirements, and introduce new regulatory tools. In this Comment, we argue that these changes are generally well-targeted but leave specific challenges for innovative artificial intelligence-enabled medical devices unresolved.

title: Machine Learning Approaches to Biologic Therapy Response in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Review Article.
desc: [Sage open pathology] Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, remains a complex and heterogeneous condition with variable response to biologic therapies. Despite significant advances with anti-TNF agents, integrin inhibitors, and interleukin-12/23 blockers, treatment outcomes are limited by primary nonresponse, secondary loss of efficacy, immunogenicity, and substantial healthcare costs. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, offers new opportunities to address these challenges by integrating diverse clinical, laboratory, imaging, histologic, genetic, and microbiome data. Recent studies demonstrate that AI-based models achieve high accuracy in predicting biologic response, remission, and adverse outcomes, outperforming conventional statistical approaches. AI has also shown promise in real-time endoscopic assessment, histologic grading, and forecasting disease progression, enabling earlier intervention and personalized therapy. However, current models are constrained by limited datasets, heterogeneity, lack of large-scale prospective validation, and concerns regarding interpretability, transparency, and patient privacy. Future efforts should prioritize multicenter trials, external validation, and ethical integration into clinical workflows. Collectively, AI-driven prediction of biologic therapy response represents a pivotal step toward precision medicine in IBD, with the potential to optimize therapeutic strategies, reduce ineffective treatment exposure, and improve patient outcomes.

title: Multimodal Deep Learning Based on Chest CT and Clinical Features for Predicting the Risk of Postoperative Pulmonary Complications: A Decision Curve Analysis
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University; conditions: Postoperative Pulmonary Complications (PPCs); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 1500; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] Background and Objective Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are common after elective colorectal surgery and are associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased morbidity, and delayed recovery. Existing PPC prediction tools were mainly developed in thoracic or mixed surgical populations and rely predominantly on clinical variables; preoperative chest CT information remains underused, and a population-specific tool for elderly colorectal cancer patients is still lacking. This study aims to develop and validate a multimodal deep learning model that integrates preoperative chest CT-derived features with multidimensional clinical variables to predict PPCs in patients aged ≥65 years undergoing elective radical colorectal cancer surgery, and to quantify its incremental value and clinical net benefit. Methods This is a single-center retrospective cohort study. Eligible patients will be assigned to a development window (August 2020-August 2024), split chronologically at a 7∶1∶2 ratio into training, validation, and test sets with five-fold cross-validation, and a locked temporal external validation window (September 2024-September 2026), which will be used only after the final model is fixed. The primary outcome is 30-day composite PPCs defined according to the EPCO criteria; the Melbourne Group Scale will serve as a parallel sensitivity definition. Preoperative clinical variables and chest CT images obtained within four weeks before surgery will be collected. A convolutional neural network imaging branch-or 2D transfer learning based on RadImageNet if the sample size is insufficient-will extract CT deep features, which will be fused with clinical variables at the feature (intermediate) level. Six classifiers, including logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and multilayer perceptron, will be tuned within a unified search space. Discrimination (AUC with DeLong test and Bootstrap 95% CI), calibration (calibration curves, Brier score), incremental value (NRI, IDI), and clinical utility (decision curve analysis) will be evaluated against the ARISCAT and GSU-Pulmonary scores, a clinical-only model, and an imaging-only model. Grad-CAM and SHAP will be applied to interpret the model. title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
desc: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
desc: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

title: Learning spatial cellular state through 3D reconstruction of the cell
desc: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

title: Recording sampling rate as a negative-control exposure for detecting measurement-driven bias in heart-rate-variability-outcome associations: a quantitative bias analysis across ICU waveform databases
desc: Importance. Heart-rate variability (HRV) is studied extensively as a prognostic marker in critical illness, yet the electrocardiographic sampling rate at which HRV is computed systematically distorts the resulting values. Whether the associations between HRV and clinical outcomes reported in the literature are partly a consequence of this distortion has not been examined directly. Objective. To evaluate whether between-database differences in native ECG sampling rate can be used as a negative-control exposure to detect measurement-driven bias in HRV-outcome associations, and to quantify the sensitivity of a published association to an empirically measured distortion coefficient using quantitative bias analysis (QBA). Design. A methods investigation in three parts. Part I sets out the causal structure and states why a strict instrumental-variable (IV) design is inappropriate here. Part II derives a bias-correction factor under a multiplicative measurement-error model and propagates the empirical confidence interval of the distortion coefficient as a sensitivity band. Part III applies the procedure to an observed HRV-mortality association from a single ICU waveform database, and examines the separate bias arising from threshold-based categorisation. Setting and data sources. Two critical-care waveform databases with different native sampling rates (MIMIC-IV Waveform, approximately 250 Hz; MIMIC-III Waveform Matched p04, 125 Hz) and an independent 500-Hz reference cohort (PTB-XL) for mechanism validation. The outcome association was estimated in 1,445 ICU stays from MIMIC-III p04, of whom 141 died in hospital (9.8%). Exposures. Native ECG sampling rate as a negative-control exposure; SDNN, RMSSD and heart rate as the measured exposures whose associations with mortality are evaluated. Main outcomes and measures. In-hospital mortality. Distortion coefficients were obtained by end-to-end reprocessing of 7,293 original waveform segments with a fixed QRS detector. Corrected odds ratios were reported as QBA sensitivity bands rather than point-identified effects. Misclassification was quantified as the proportion of recordings below a 20 ms HRV threshold reclassified above it by coarse sampling. Results.
